name: Hana Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is your usual shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Hana, 58, and I run a small coffee-roasting drum at a food factory. I finished secondary school and moved from bag packing onto the roaster eight months ago, so I still ask the lead to check my first temperature curve. I like hearing the beans crack at the right moment, but I have scorched a batch by opening the door too late.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do the job and family money fit, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Farid works regular hospital porter shifts, and our children are grown and living elsewhere. I earn about the normal rate for a roaster operator, we have four months of expenses saved and some other food plants nearby. I use AI every day to explain roast-log patterns, then compare them with the colour and smell of a sample. We talk about retirement, but we have not matched any estimate to our actual bills yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AI can tidy roast logs, but the beans still have to be cooled and checked before they go into bags. A little help with order sheets would leave our shift much the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two regular wages cover rent and food, and four months saved gives us breathing room. The mild AI picture would not threaten my hours, though I am still learning how this drum behaves after a dark roast. I can ask a person on the line when a graph looks odd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep running the roaster and showing the first cooling tray to the lead. I already use AI each day to read logs, so I would carry on checking its ideas against the beans; I would add a small new amount from each full paid month to our reserve after bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The machine would still need my hands, and Farid's hospital wage is steady at the moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did a log fail to tell you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week the curve looked fine, but the first tray smelled burnt because I had left the drum door closed too long. I held the batch while the lead checked it. A clean roast graph cannot take the burnt taste out of a coffee bean.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you add to the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only from new pay after rent, food and power. The four months already saved would stay for a gap in wages; moving them to another account would not build a new cushion.

say: I would say **coffee beans** still need physical checks after a tidy AI log.
A **cooling-tray sample** tells us more than an order sheet about a batch.
think: Our **regular wages** and four-month reserve make this mild picture secure.
I can still ask a **human lead** when the roast curve looks strange.
do: **Keep** running the coffee roaster and showing first cooled beans to the lead.
**Save** a new amount from full paid months after rent and food.
feel: **Calm** about current paid work while still learning the roaster.
S0.quote: A clean roast graph cannot take the burnt taste out of a coffee bean.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI habit** is established log reading, with colour and smell used to test each suggestion.
The **fresh savings** come from future full pay; the existing four-month reserve remains available for income gaps.

steps.text: Keep roasting coffee and checking first cooling tray with lead
Save new money from full paid months after household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI may write orders and plan roast runs before capable robots can empty a hot drum. I would want a paid test of any new bean camera before it changes how many operators the shift needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am still junior on the roaster, so one person watching two drums could make my hours shrink. Four months saved and Farid's porter pay give us time, but my wage matters for the rent. I am willing to learn the camera if its mistakes are shown, not hidden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would practise a new AI bean-defect classifier on archived rejected trays if the plant gives paid time and the lead checks the labels. If a funded roaster-control course offers a real paid supervised place on an isolated drum, I would take it. If my base shifts are cut, I would apply only to posted nearby food-machine jobs with safe duties, base pay and travel that cover our household bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible cut to my own paid hours, even with savings. I would rather find a false reject in the training room than after a pallet is shipped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which beans would test the camera?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use a tray of good beans, one under-roasted tray and one with a scorched edge, then ask the lead to check my labels. A camera lesson should have bad beans on the table, not only pictures on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must the course include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trainer must show me how to isolate the drum, check the cooling gate and restart on a test load. A paid place without guarded practice is only a seat in a room.

say: I would ask for **paid camera tests** before reducing a roast shift.
A **guarded roaster lesson** needs an actual trainer and isolated drum.
think: My **junior hours** could shrink if one operator watches two drums.
Four months saved and **Farid's wage** help, but do not replace my rent money.
do: **Practise** new AI bean labels only on paid archived tests with lead review.
**Take** a funded roaster course if an isolated paid supervised place is offered.
**Apply** after actual cuts to posted safe nearby machine jobs if pay and travel cover bills.
feel: **Anxious** about a realistic roster cut, while curious about a tested camera.
S1.quote: A camera lesson should have bad beans on the table, not only pictures on a screen.
fieldNote: She separates **new AI learning** on rejected beans from the daily log explanations she already uses.
The **course and search** depend on a safe paid place or posted local work with sufficient base pay and travel.

steps.text: Practise new AI bean classifier only on paid archived trays with lead review
Take roaster-control course if funded paid isolated trainer place offered
Apply after base cuts to posted safe nearby food-machine jobs if pay and travel fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Farid that AGI could plan roast orders by 2028, while capable robots that empty and inspect the physical drums follow around 2031. I would ask our plant to name which paid jobs remain before it replaces the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when the robots can work the hot drum. I expect the newer operators, including me, to lose many shifts. Farid's wage and four months saved would not cover our rent and bills for long; I would be awake counting what happens after the fourth month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would cancel the planned weekend trip before paying its balance and put a new part of each full wage into the cash reserve while I still have work. If a recognised coffee-quality course is offered with funded fees, paid release and guarded hands-on testing, I would enrol. After qualifying, if my roaster hours fall, I would apply to posted safe local quality jobs only if regular pay and travel cover our bills; if no course is offered, I would apply to posted safe food-packing jobs on those same terms while keeping any paid roast shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed by the likely loss of most of my work. Four months is time to search, but not a retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a safe quality test teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check colour and weight on a cooled tray, reject a scorched batch and stop the drum before reaching inside. A trainer must watch the stop on a guarded machine before I touch a live load.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop working at 63?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for actual retirement-income figures and compare them with rent, food and heat. If the numbers do not cover those bills, I would keep applying for paid work rather than retire on an assumed date.

say: I would separate **2028 order planning** from physical coffee-roasting robots around 2031.
I would ask the plant for **written paid-role dates** before replacing the drum line.
think: At **63**, I expect newer roast shifts, including mine, to shrink.
Four months saved and one **porter wage** cannot cover our bills indefinitely.
do: **Cancel** the trip balance and save fresh full-shift pay in cash.
**Enrol** in recognised quality instruction only if fees, release and guarded practice are funded.
**Apply** after lost hours to posted safe quality if qualified, or packing without a course, at bill-covering pay.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless cash-gap calculations.
S2.quote: Four months is time to search, but not a retirement plan.
fieldNote: Her **physical risk** begins around 2031 when capable robots can empty and inspect drums, after 2028 thinking AI changes orders.
The **quality and packing** applications need separate real safe postings; retirement depends on figures not yet known.

steps.text: Cancel planned weekend trip before paying balance
Save part of new full-shift wages in cash reserve
Enrol in recognised coffee-quality course if funded paid guarded practical place offered
Apply after cuts for posted safe local quality if qualified or packing without course; pay/travel fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AGI may plan roast batches in 2031, while capable robots that handle hot drums follow around 2034. Five years gives us time to see which practical courses and paid posts are real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 when the robots can do the physical work. I might still need my wage then; our four months saved will not decide when we can afford to retire. A qualification could help if the food plants actually hire quality checkers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the roast shifts and add new money from each offered paid extra day after bills. If a locally accepted food-quality certificate offers funded fees, paid time and supervised practice at a stopped roaster, I would enrol. After passing, if roast hours fall, I would apply to posted safe local quality jobs only if base pay and travel cover our bills; without a course place, I would look for posted packing work under the same terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the later roster, but I can test the course before leaving paid work. I enjoy learning, provided the qualification has an employer at the other end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the practical exam make you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would weigh a cooled sample, identify a burnt bean and stop the drum safely before a trainer signs the test. The first bad batch should be caught at the factory, not in a customer's cup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check that employers accept the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask two food plants for their actual quality-job requirements and compare them with the certificate. If neither accepts it, I would keep my wage and look for another offered course.

say: I would ask for **accepted practical courses** before robots reach hot roasting around 2034.
A **quality vacancy** needs real posted wages, not only a course promise.
think: At **66**, I may still need paid work despite a longer warning.
A **recognised certificate** helps only if local food plants hire for it.
do: **Save** new wages from offered extra roast days after bills.
**Enrol** only in locally accepted quality training with funded fees, paid time and stopped-machine practice.
**Apply** after qualifying and cuts to posted safe quality, or packing without training, at bill-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious** about later shifts, with time to verify a paid route.
S3.quote: The first bad batch should be caught at the factory, not in a customer's cup.
fieldNote: Her **course acceptance** depends on local employers' real requirements, funded fees, paid time and supervised stopped-roaster practice.
Both **job routes** need safe local postings and base pay that still covers bills after travel.

steps.text: Save new money from offered extra roast days after bills
Enrol in accepted quality course if funded paid stopped-roaster place offered
Apply for posted safe local quality if qualified and cut, base pay and travel fit
Search posted safe local packing if no course, base pay and travel fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI might plan coffee orders in 2036, and capable robots could handle the roaster around 2039. A decade gives us time to check the pension figures and the jobs that actually pay; it does not guarantee either one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 71 when those physical robots arrive, if I am still on the factory roster. Farid and I may be able to stop earlier, but only if written retirement income covers our living costs. Our current work and four-month reserve make the near years manageable, while the far end remains unsettled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep running the roaster while it pays and request written retirement-income and cost figures this year. I would enrol in a locally accepted coffee-quality course only if fees, paid release and supervised safe practice are offered. If I am still employed after 2036 and roast hours fall, I would apply only to posted safe local quality or packing work whose base pay and travel cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the far end, not frightened for next month. I can enjoy a new control now without pretending it settles our retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What number would decide whether you could stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Farid and I would add the written retirement amounts and compare them with rent, food, power and medical costs. If the total falls short, I would plan to keep earning rather than announce a leaving date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your grown children to cover the difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might ask them to help read a confusing form, but they have their own households. I would not put an assumed payment from them into our budget.

say: I would separate **2036 coffee planning** from physical roaster robots around 2039.
A **decade of warning** does not guarantee retirement income or paid jobs.
think: At **71**, I may already have stopped work if the figures permit it.
Our **current wages** and four-month reserve make the near years sound, not the distant outcome certain.
do: **Keep** paid roast shifts while checking written retirement income and costs.
**Enrol** only in locally accepted quality training with funded paid supervised safe practice.
**Apply** after 2036 cuts if still employed to posted safe local work with bill-covering pay and travel.
feel: **Uneasy** about distant work and retirement, with near-term income intact.
S4.quote: I can enjoy a new control now without pretending it settles our retirement.
fieldNote: A **retirement enquiry** asks whether actual income covers costs; no statutory payment or exit date is assumed.
Training needs an **accepted funded place**, while any later job search requires current employment, cut hours and safe posted pay.

steps.text: Keep paid coffee-roaster shifts while they remain
Request written retirement income and cost figures this year
Enrol in accepted quality course if funded paid supervised safe place offered
Apply after 2036 cuts if employed to posted safe local work if pay and travel fit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robots around 2031 could remove my new roasting shift before we know whether retirement income covers our bills. A real funded quality course, written job dates and posted safe local work at usable base pay would help. I would need actual pension figures before considering an exit.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who tastes the first beans when a robot empties the drum. A roast chart is useful, but the burnt taste has to be found before anyone buys the bag. I want that check paid for, whoever performs it.

headlineQuote: A roast chart is useful, but the burnt taste has to be found before anyone buys the bag.
portrait: **Hana**, 58, is a junior coffee-roaster operator with secondary education who is still learning the drum after a move from packing.
She and her **hospital-porter partner** Farid have grown children, typical operator pay and four months of expenses saved.
She uses **AI daily** for roast logs but checks real beans, and takes new controls and training only with safe paid evidence.
Fast **2031 robots** alarm her about lost shifts; longer runways permit accepted training and retirement decisions based on written income figures.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring capable roasting robots around 2031 before she knows whether retirement income covers bills.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **funded practical training**, written job dates, posted safe local work and actual retirement-income figures.
